So here is the plan for a line like this. Hunt for times and divide and do those first. Then do the plus and minus, from left to right.
Here is our sum. 24 minus 4 times 4, plus 1. Three different signs, so the order we work in really matters.
Where shall we start?

ask.ifNot: Look for the times sign. Times comes before plus and minus, so 4 times 4 goes first, wherever it sits in the line.

beats.say: I'll underline 4 times 4, because times is done before plus and minus. 4 times 4 is 16.
Now we write the line again, with 16 sitting where 4 times 4 was. Everything else stays put.
Two signs left, a minus and a plus. Which pair goes next?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equally strong, so neither jumps the queue. We simply go from left to right, and 24 minus 16 is on the left.

beats.say: 24 minus 16 is 8. Careful here: the minus belongs only to the 16. The plus 1 must not get swallowed up with it.
Last step. 8 plus 1 makes 9. That is our answer.
Remember it like this. Times and divide go first, wherever they sit. Plus and minus wait their turn, then go from left to right.
Let's write it up. 16 divided by 2, plus 5 times 2. Three signs, so we need to think about the order.
Which parts have to be done before the plus?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times are both stronger than plus. So both of those pairs are worked out first, and the plus waits in the middle until they are done.

beats.say: Both of these beat the plus. First the divide: 16 divided by 2 is 8.
And the other pair: 5 times 2 makes 10.
Now we write the line again with those two answers in place. It has shrunk to 8 plus 10.
At last the plus gets its turn. 8 plus 10 is 18. That is our answer.
Here is the trap. Working along from the left, one step at a time, is like wrapping a bracket round the first part. That gives 26, which belongs to a different sum.
So here is the plan for a line like this. Hunt for times and divide and do those first. Then do the plus and minus, from left to right.
Let's write this one up. 27 times 9, plus 14. Before we work anything out, we decide where to start.
Which pair of numbers goes first?

ask.ifNot: 9 plus 14 looks like the easier bit, so it is tempting. But times is stronger than plus, so 27 times 9 has to go first.

beats.say: Times comes before plus, so I'll underline this pair. 27 times 9 is easier in two bites, so let's split 27 into 20 and 7.
20 times 9 is 180, and 7 times 9 is 63. Put them together and we get 243.
So 27 times 9 has turned into 243, and the plus 14 is still waiting at the end.
And 243 plus 14 is 257. That is our answer.
See the trap? If the 9 plus 14 went first, as if it wore a bracket, the line would come to 621. That belongs to a different sum.
So here is the plan for a line like this. Hunt for times and divide and do those first. Then do the plus and minus, from left to right.
Look at this one. 49 minus 2 times 10, plus 5. Before we work anything out, we need to decide where to start.
So, which part do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Look for the times sign. Times comes before plus and minus, so 2 times 10 goes first, wherever it sits in the line.

beats.say: I'll underline 2 times 10, because times is done before plus and minus. 2 times 10 is 20.
Now we write the line again, with 20 sitting where 2 times 10 was. Everything else stays put.
Now there is only a minus and a plus. Which of these do we do next?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equally strong, so neither jumps the queue. We simply go from left to right, and 49 minus 20 is on the left.

beats.say: Left to right, so 49 minus 20 first, and that is 29. Watch out: we are taking away 20 only, not 20 and 5 together.
And 29 plus 5 is 34. So the whole line comes to 34.
Remember it like this. Times and divide go first, wherever they sit. Plus and minus wait their turn, then go from left to right.
Look at this line. 17 times 3, plus 3. Short, but it still has an order to follow.
Have a look at the two signs. Where do we start?

ask.ifNot: Look for the times sign. Times comes before plus, so 17 times 3 goes first.

beats.say: I'll underline 17 times 3, because times goes before plus. To make it easier, we break 17 into 10 and 7.
10 times 3 is 30, and 7 times 3 is 21. Put them together and we get 51.
So 17 times 3 has turned into 51, and the plus 3 is still waiting at the end.
Now it is easy. 51 plus 3 makes 54.
See the trap? If the 3 plus 3 went first, as if it wore a bracket, the line would come to 102. That belongs to a different sum.
So here is the plan for a line like this. Hunt for times and divide and do those first. Then do the plus and minus, from left to right.
Look at this line. 22 plus 6 times 2. A plus and a times, side by side.
Have a look at the two signs. Where do we start?

ask.ifNot: Look for the times sign. Times comes before plus, so 6 times 2 goes first, even though it sits at the end of the line.

beats.say: I'll underline 6 times 2, because times is always done before plus. 6 times 2 is 12.
So 6 times 2 turns into 12, and the 22 in front comes down unchanged.
And 22 plus 12 is 34. That is our answer.
Here is why the order matters. Adding 22 and 6 first is like putting a bracket round them, and that gives 56. A different sum, so a different answer.
So here is the plan for a line like this. Hunt for times and divide and do those first. Then do the plus and minus, from left to right.
Let's write it up. 47 minus 2 times 5, plus 2. A minus, a times and a plus, all in one line.
Have a look at the signs. Which pair of numbers goes first?

ask.ifNot: Starting from the left with 47 minus 2 is the natural thing to try. But times is stronger than plus and minus, so 2 times 5 has to go first.

beats.say: I'll underline 2 times 5, because times is done before plus and minus. 2 times 5 is 10.
So 2 times 5 turns into 10, and the rest of the line comes down unchanged.
Two signs left, a minus and a plus. Which pair goes next?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equally strong, so neither jumps the queue. We simply go from left to right, and 47 minus 10 is on the left.

beats.say: Left to right, so 47 minus 10 first, and that is 37. Watch out: we are taking away 10 only, not 10 and 2 together.
And 37 plus 2 is 39. So the whole line comes to 39.
That is the whole trick. Before you work anything out, look at the signs. Times and divide first, then plus and minus in order.
Look at this line. 29 times 6, plus 7. Short, but it still has an order to follow.
Have a look at the two signs. Where do we start?

ask.ifNot: Look for the times sign. Times comes before plus, so 29 times 6 goes first.

beats.say: I'll underline 29 times 6, because times goes before plus. To make it easier, we break 29 into 20 and 9.
20 times 6 is 120, and 9 times 6 is 54. Put them together and we get 174.
Now we write the line again, with 174 sitting where 29 times 6 was. The plus 7 comes down unchanged.
Now it is easy. 174 plus 7 makes 181.
See the trap? If the 6 plus 7 went first, as if it wore a bracket, the line would come to 377. That belongs to a different sum.
Remember it like this. Times and divide go first, wherever they sit. Plus and minus wait their turn, then go from left to right.
Here is our sum. 15 plus 6 times 1. Only two signs, but there is a trap hiding in it.
Before we work anything out: which pair of numbers goes first?

ask.ifNot: Starting on the left with 15 plus 6 is the natural thing to try. But times is stronger than plus, so 6 times 1 has to go first.

beats.say: I'll underline 6 times 1, because times is always done before plus. 6 times 1 is just 6.
So 6 times 1 turns into 6, and the 15 in front comes down unchanged.
And 15 plus 6 is 21. That is our answer.
Times 1 changes nothing, so this one was kind to us. With any other number there, starting from the left would have gone astray.
Remember it like this. Times and divide go first, wherever they sit. Plus and minus wait their turn, then go from left to right.
Look at this one. 42 minus 2 times 2, plus 3. Before we work anything out, we need to decide where to start.
Where shall we start?

ask.ifNot: Starting from the left with 42 minus 2 is the natural thing to try. But times is stronger than plus and minus, so 2 times 2 has to go first.

beats.say: Times comes before plus and minus, so this pair goes first. I'll underline it. 2 times 2 is 4.
So 2 times 2 turns into 4, and the rest of the line comes down unchanged.
Two signs left, a minus and a plus. Which pair goes next?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equally strong, so neither jumps the queue. We simply go from left to right, and 42 minus 4 is on the left.

beats.say: Left to right, so 42 minus 4 first, and that is 38. Watch out: we are taking away 4 only, not 4 and 3 together.
Last step. 38 plus 3 makes 41. That is our answer.
So here is the plan for a line like this. Hunt for times and divide and do those first. Then do the plus and minus, from left to right.
Look at this one. 30 divided by 3, plus 2 times 3. Before we work anything out, we decide what goes first.
The plus sits in the middle. What must we work out before we can use it?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times are both stronger than plus. So both of those pairs are worked out first, and the plus waits in the middle until they are done.

beats.say: Divide and times both come before plus. Let's take them one at a time. 30 divided by 3 is 10.
And the other pair: 2 times 3 makes 6.
Now we write the line again with those two answers in place. It has shrunk to 10 plus 6.
At last the plus gets its turn. 10 plus 6 is 16. That is our answer.
Here is the trap. Working along from the left, one step at a time, is like wrapping a bracket round the first part. That gives 36, which belongs to a different sum.
Remember it like this. Times and divide go first, wherever they sit. Plus and minus wait their turn, then go from left to right.
Look at this line. 29 times 7, plus 11. Short, but it still has an order to follow.
Have a look at the two signs. Where do we start?

ask.ifNot: 7 plus 11 looks like the easier bit, so it is tempting. But times is stronger than plus, so 29 times 7 has to go first.

beats.say: I'll underline 29 times 7, because times goes before plus. To make it easier, we break 29 into 20 and 9.
20 times 7 is 140, and 9 times 7 is 63. Put them together and we get 203.
So 29 times 7 has turned into 203, and the plus 11 is still waiting at the end.
And 203 plus 11 is 214. That is our answer.
Here is why the order matters. Doing 7 plus 11 first is like putting a bracket round them, and that gives 522. A different sum, so a different answer.
That is the whole trick. Before you work anything out, look at the signs. Times and divide first, then plus and minus in order.
Let's write it up. 2 x, plus 5, equals 17. The x is a number in disguise, and our job is to unmask it.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 2 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 2 x has a plus 5 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: The opposite of plus 5 is minus 5. So we take away 5, and we do it on both sides so the balance stays level.
On the left, plus 5 and minus 5 cancel each other out. On the right, 17 minus 5 leaves 12.
Now 2 x is 2 lots of x. How do we get from 2 lots down to just one?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2.
12 divided by 2 is 6. So x equals 6. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 6 back in place of x. 2 times 6 is 12, and 12 plus 5 is 17. It works.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added or taken off. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Look at this equation. 8 x, plus 20, equals 100. We want the x all on its own, so we can see what it is.
The two sides balance, like a see-saw. We want the 8 x alone on its side. What do we clear away first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 8 x has a plus 20 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: To undo plus 20, we take away 20. And to keep the balance level, we do it to both sides.
The left side is now just 8 x. The right side is 100 minus 20, which is 80.
Now 8 x is 8 lots of x. How do we get from 8 lots down to just one?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 8, we divide by 8.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 8.
80 shared into 8 equal parts gives 10 each. So x equals 10. Found it!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 10 back in place of x. 8 times 10 is 80, and 80 plus 20 is 100. It works.
Two moves, every time. Undo the plus or minus first, then undo the times. And always do the same to both sides.
Here is our equation. 2 x, minus 6, equals 10. Somewhere behind that x a number is hiding, and we are going to find it.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 2 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 2 x has a minus 6 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: To undo minus 6, we add 6. And to keep the balance level, we do it to both sides.
The left side is now just 2 x. The right side is 10 plus 6, which is 16.
Now 2 x is 2 lots of x. How do we get from 2 lots down to just one?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2.
16 shared into 2 equal parts gives 8 each. So x equals 8. Found it!
Let's check it. With 8 in place of x, 2 times 8 is 16. Then 16 minus 6 gives 10, just as the equation says.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added or taken off. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Three bags hold 24 apples between them. We know two totals for pairs of bags, and we want the first and third bags together.
All three bags hold 24. The first and second together hold 11. What does that tell us about the third bag?

ask.ifNot: The three bags make 24. Take away the first two, which hold 11 between them, and what is left must be in the third bag.

beats.say: 24 minus 11 is 13. The third bag holds 13 apples.
Now the same idea from the other end. The second and third together hold 18, so the first bag holds 24 minus 18, which is 6.
First and third together: 6 plus 13 is 19.
Let's check with the second bag. It must hold 24 minus 19, which is 5. Then 6 plus 5 is 11, and 5 plus 13 is 18. Both clues fit.
When you know the whole and one part, subtract to find the rest. Here we simply did that twice.
A boy played for 1 hour and 15 minutes. We want that as a decimal number of hours.
It is tempting to put the 15 straight after the point. Why does that not work?

ask.ifNot: A decimal counts in tenths and hundredths. But minutes are sixtieths of an hour. So 15 minutes is 15 out of 60, not 15 out of 100.

beats.say: So 15 minutes is 15 out of 60 of an hour. 15 goes into 60 exactly 4 times, so that is one quarter of an hour.

spec.note: A quarter of the way round

beats.say: And one quarter is 25 hundredths, which we write as 0.25.
So the time is 1 whole hour plus 0.25 of an hour. That is 1.25 hours.
Check it backwards. 0.25 of 60 minutes is 15 minutes. Just right.
To turn minutes into hours, divide by 60 first. Never just write the minutes after the point.
A line with decimals in it, and four different signs. The order matters just as much with decimals.
Which parts do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times come before plus and minus. So the 4.2 divided by 6 and the 0.3 times 0.4 are both done first.

beats.say: First the divide. 42 divided by 6 is 7, so 4.2 divided by 6 is 0.7.
Now the times. 3 times 4 is 12. There are two decimal places in the question, one in each number, so the answer has two as well: 0.12.
Write the line again with those two answers in place.
Now left to right. 8 minus 0.7 is 7.3.
7.3 is the same as 7.30. Add 0.12 and we get 7.42.
Same rule as always: times and divide first, then plus and minus from left to right. And count the decimal places when you multiply.
Four little sums made of 9s and 3s. We want the one with the least value, so let's work out each.
The first one. Times goes first: 9 times 3 is 27, and 27 plus 3 is 30.
The second. 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 plus 9 is 18.
The fourth has a bracket, so that goes first. 9 plus 3 is 12, and 12 times 3 is 36.
Now the third one, 9 minus 3 times 3. Which part goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times comes before minus. So 3 times 3 goes first, even though the minus is on the left.

beats.say: 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 minus 9 is 0.
So the values are 30, 18, 0 and 36. Nothing here is smaller than 0, so the third one is the least.
Work out every choice in the proper order before you compare. One slip in the order can change which one wins.
A man bought 27 eggs. We want to say that in dozens, as a decimal.
How many full dozens fit into 27?

ask.ifNot: Count in 12s. Two 12s still fit inside 27, but a third 12 would go past it.

beats.say: 2 dozens use up 24 eggs. That leaves 3 eggs over.
Those 3 left-over eggs are only part of a dozen. What fraction of a dozen are they?

ask.ifNot: A dozen has 12 eggs, so 3 eggs are 3 out of 12, not 3 out of 10. This is exactly where the decimal trap hides.

beats.say: 3 out of 12 is one quarter. And one quarter, as a decimal, is 0.25.
So 27 eggs are 2 dozens and 0.25 of a dozen. That is 2.25 dozen.
Check: 2.25 times 12 should take us back to 27 eggs. It does.
The leftovers become a fraction of the group size, here twelfths. Then turn that fraction into a decimal.
Three boxes to fill with signs, so that the line comes to 28.
We test each set, always doing times and divide before plus and minus. First set: plus, times, divide. Which part goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide come before plus. And between a times and a divide we go from left to right, so 6 times 4 is first.

beats.say: 6 times 4 is 24. Then 24 divided by 6 is 4, and 10 plus 4 is 14. Not 28.
Second set: plus, minus, divide. That needs 4 divided by 6, which is not a whole number. So this line cannot land exactly on 28.
Third set: plus, times, minus. Times first again: 6 times 4 is 24.
Now left to right. 10 plus 24 is 34, and 34 minus 6 is 28. That is the one.
So the signs are plus, times, minus. For box puzzles, test each set and follow the proper order every time.
A man bought 21 oranges. We want to write that as a decimal number of dozens.
21 is more than one dozen but less than two. So there is one full dozen, and 9 oranges left over.
What fraction of a dozen are those 9 left-over oranges?

ask.ifNot: A full dozen is 12 oranges, so 9 oranges are 9 out of 12. Using 9 out of 10 would be thinking in tens, not dozens.

beats.say: 9 out of 12. Divide the top and the bottom by 3, and it becomes three quarters.
One quarter is 0.25. So what is three quarters as a decimal?

ask.ifNot: Three quarters is 3 lots of one quarter. And 3 lots of 0.25 make 0.75.

beats.say: So 21 oranges are 1 dozen and 0.75 of a dozen. That is 1.75 dozen.
Check: 1.75 times 12 gives back 21 oranges.
The tempting slip is to pop the 21 straight into a decimal. That would only be right if a dozen were 10. Leftovers are twelfths.
Round, curly and square brackets, all in one line. We open them from the inside out.
Which part do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Brackets come before everything, and the innermost bracket comes first of all. That is the round one, 3 plus 2.

beats.say: 3 plus 2 is 5.
Next the curly bracket: 2 minus 5. We are taking away more than we have. What do we get?

ask.ifNot: From 2, taking away 2 gets us down to 0. There are still 3 more to take away, so we finish 3 below zero. We write minus 3.

beats.say: So the curly bracket is worth minus 3.
Inside the square bracket, times first: 2 times 3 is 6. Then 6 minus, minus 3. Taking away a minus number is the same as adding, so that is 6 plus 3, which is 9.
No brackets left. Divide goes before plus and minus: 6 divided by 2 is 3.
Left to right now. 8 plus 3 is 11, and 11 minus 9 is 2.
Innermost bracket first and work outwards. Then divide and times. Then plus and minus, left to right.
A two-digit number ending in 9, times a three-digit number ending in 3. The other digits are hidden. Which of the four choices could be the product?
The usual first test is the last digit. 9 times 3 is 27, so the product ends in 7. But look: all four choices end in 7! What else can we test?

choices: how big the product can be
ask.ifNot: We know how many digits each number has. So we can work out the smallest and the biggest the product could possibly be.

beats.say: Smallest first. The smallest two-digit number ending in 9 is 19. The smallest three-digit number ending in 3 is 103. And 19 times 103 is 1957.
So nothing below 1957 is possible. That rules out 957, and it rules out 1907 as well, by just a whisker.
Now the biggest. 99 times 993 is 98307, which has five digits. So the six-digit number 756927 is far too big.
Only 46847 is left. And it really works: 79 times 593 is 46847.
When the last-digit test cannot separate the choices, test the size: the smallest and the biggest the product could be.
We are handed a fact for free: 21 times 24 is 504. The new sum has the same digits, just with decimal points in them.
So the digits of the answer will be 5, 0, 4 again. We only have to place the point. First, how did 21 turn into 2.1?

ask.ifNot: The point has moved one place to the left, which makes the number 10 times smaller. That is dividing by 10.

beats.say: 21 was divided by 10. And 24 became 0.24: the point moved two places, so it was divided by 100.
So the answer is 504 made 10 times smaller, and then 100 times smaller again. Altogether that is 1000 times smaller.
Dividing by 1000 moves the point three places to the left. 504 becomes 0.504.
A quick way to see it: count the decimal places in the question. One in 2.1 and two in 0.24 makes three, so the answer has three decimal places.
When you are given a multiplication fact, keep the digits and just work out where the point belongs.
One long sum divided by another. We could add them both up, but let's look at the numbers first.
What do you notice about every number here?

ask.ifNot: 66 is 6 elevens, 77 is 7 elevens, and so on. Every number here is in the 11 times table.

beats.say: So the top is 6 elevens, 7 elevens, 8 elevens and 9 elevens. 6 plus 7 plus 8 plus 9 is 30, so the top is 30 elevens.
The bottom is 1, 2, 3 and 4 elevens. That makes 10 elevens.
So we have 30 elevens divided by 10 elevens. What is that?

ask.ifNot: The elevens are the same on the top and on the bottom, so they cancel out. We are left with 30 divided by 10.

beats.say: 30 divided by 10 is 3.
The long way agrees. The top adds to 330, the bottom to 110, and 330 divided by 110 is 3.
Before a long calculation, look for something all the numbers share. It can shrink the work to almost nothing.
We are given one fact, and asked a sum that looks very like it. Same digits, different decimal points.
Compare the two. 15 has become 1.5, which is 10 times smaller. And 0.005 has become 0.05. Is that bigger or smaller, and by how much?

ask.ifNot: 0.005 is 5 thousandths, and 0.05 is 5 hundredths. Hundredths are 10 times bigger than thousandths, so that number became 10 times bigger.

beats.say: One number went 10 times smaller, the other 10 times bigger. Those two changes cancel each other out, so the product stays the same.
Now the last part, times 100. Multiplying by 100 shifts every digit two places to the left, so the point seems to hop two places to the right.
A check on the middle step. 15 times 5 is 75, and 1.5 times 0.05 has three decimal places in it, so it is 0.075. Good.
When a new sum has the same digits as a fact you know, don't start again. Just track how each number has grown or shrunk.
Four sums made from 19 and 5. Exactly one of them comes to 100.
The first one. Times goes before minus: 5 times 5 is 25. And 19 minus 25 drops below zero. Not 100.
The second. Bracket first: 19 minus 5 is 14, and 14 times 5 is 70. Not 100.
The third. 19 plus 5 is 24, and 24 times 5 is 120. Too big.
That leaves the last one, 19 times 5 plus 5. Let's make sure. Which part goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times comes before plus. Adding 5 and 5 first would turn it into 19 times 10, which is a different sum.

beats.say: 19 times 5. An easy way: 20 times 5 is 100, then take away one 5. That leaves 95.
And 95 plus 5 is 100. This is the one.
You can also see it in one glance: 19 fives and one more five make 20 fives. Work each choice in the proper order, and brackets first.
A long multiplication gives a number of minutes, and we want to know how many weeks that is.
We could multiply it all out, but let's be clever and leave it as a product. First, how many minutes are in one week?

ask.ifNot: A week is 7 days. Each day is 24 hours. Each hour is 60 minutes. So we multiply all three.

beats.say: Now hunt for those same pieces inside our product. There is a 7 already. And 6 times 4 makes the 24.
What is left over? 8, 5, 3, 2 and 1. 8 times 5 is 40. Then 40 times 3 times 2 is 240.
And 240 is 60 times 4. So there is our 60, with a 4 to spare.
So our product is 7 times 24 times 60, and then times 4. How many weeks is that?

ask.ifNot: We matched the 7, the 24 and the 60 that make one week, and a 4 was left over. So it is 4 lots of a week.

beats.say: It is 4 weeks.
The long way agrees. The product is 40320 minutes, a week is 10080 minutes, and 40320 divided by 10080 is 4.
When a big product has to be divided, look for the divisor's pieces hiding inside it before you multiply anything out.
A man bought some articles, counted in dozens. One of these decimals cannot be right. Which?

board.text: Dozens of articles: which one is impossible?

beats.say: You can only buy whole articles. So when we turn the dozens into single articles, the answer must be a whole number. How do we turn dozens into articles?

ask.ifNot: Each dozen is 12 articles. So the number of articles is the number of dozens times 12.

beats.say: The 3 whole dozens are fine in every choice: that is 36 articles. So only the part after the point needs testing.
0.75 of a dozen is three quarters of 12, which is 9. Whole. 0.25 is a quarter of 12, which is 3. Whole. And 0.5 is half of 12, which is 6. Whole.
Now the last one, 0.15 of a dozen. Will that be a whole number of articles? Have a guess before we work it out.
0.15 times 12 comes to 1.8. Nobody can buy 1.8 of an article!
So 3.15 dozen would mean 37.8 articles, and that cannot happen. 3.15 is the impossible one.
A count of things must be whole. Change the dozens into single items, and see whether it comes out whole.
A three-digit number ending in 7, times a two-digit number ending in 8. Clubs hide the other digits. Which choice can be the product?
We can see only the last digits, 7 and 8. What must the product end in?

ask.ifNot: The last digit of a product comes from the last digits multiplied together. Work out 7 times 8, and look at the digit it ends in.

beats.say: 7 times 8 is 56, so the product ends in 6. That removes 29405, which ends in 5.
Three are left, all ending in 6. So test the size. The smallest numbers that fit are 107 and 18, and 107 times 18 is 1926.
1906 is smaller than that, so it is out. Only just, but out.
The biggest numbers that fit are 997 and 98. 997 times 98 is 97706. So what about 977706?

ask.ifNot: Count the digits. The biggest possible product, 97706, has five digits. 977706 has six, so it is far too big.

beats.say: Cross out 977706. Only 52606 is left, and it does work: 907 times 58 is 52606.
Last digit first, then smallest and biggest. Those two tests sort out almost every hidden-digit product.
This line is not true yet. We need to slip in one pair of brackets so that it really equals 40.
As it stands, 3 times 25 is 75, and 75 minus 13 plus 4 is 66. Too big. So the brackets must bring it down.
Let's think backwards from 40. If the plus 4 comes last, then just before it we had 36. And 36 is 3 times what?

ask.ifNot: Go up the 3 times table. You reach 36 at 3 times 12.

beats.say: So we want the 3 to multiply 12. Can we make 12 from the numbers that follow? Yes: 25 minus 13 is 12. Put the brackets there.
Brackets first: 25 minus 13 is 12. Then times: 3 times 12 is 36.
And 36 plus 4 is 40. The line is true now.
The other choices do not work. Brackets round 3 times 25 change nothing. Round 13 plus 4 we get 58, and the long bracket gives 48.
To place brackets, work backwards from the answer you need, and look for the numbers that can make it.
Five decimals. We put them in descending order, biggest first, and then add the 1st and the 4th.
To compare decimals fairly, give them all the same number of decimal places. The longest have 3 places, so we pad the others with zeros.
Now every one is a number of thousandths. Which is the biggest?

ask.ifNot: Read them as thousandths: 62, 50, 560, 34 and 7. The biggest of those is 560, so 0.560 is the biggest decimal.

beats.say: Descending order means biggest first. So: 560, 62, 50, 34, 7 thousandths.
The 1st is 0.560, which is our 0.56. Count along to the 4th, and it is 0.034.
Add them. 560 thousandths plus 34 thousandths is 594 thousandths. That is 0.594.
The trap was to think 0.062 beats 0.56 because it has more digits. Line up the decimal places and that trap disappears.
To order decimals, pad them to the same length. Then compare them like whole numbers.
This line is not true as it stands. One pair of brackets will make it equal 33.
Without brackets, times goes first. 7 times 5 is 35, and 12 minus 35 already drops below zero. Nowhere near 33.
So think backwards from 33. If the plus 8 comes last, then just before it we had 25. And 25 is 5 times what?

ask.ifNot: 5 times 5 is 25. So we need a 5 to be sitting in front of the times 5.

beats.say: We need a 5 in front of the times 5. And look: 12 minus 7 is 5! So the brackets go round 12 minus 7.
Brackets first: 12 minus 7 is 5. Then 5 times 5 is 25.
And 25 plus 8 is 33. The line is true now.
What about the other choices? Brackets round 7 times 5 change nothing. The other two only make the amount we subtract bigger, so they sink below zero as well.
To place brackets, work backwards from the answer, and see which numbers can build what you need.
A basket of 104 mangoes. Again and again we take out 4 mangoes and put in 3 apples, until no mangoes are left. How many apples then?

board.text: 104 mangoes. Each swap: 4 mangoes out, 3 apples in

beats.say: First, how many swaps does it take to clear out all the mangoes?

ask.ifNot: Each swap removes 4 mangoes. So we need to know how many 4s there are in 104, and that is a division.

beats.say: 100 divided by 4 is 25, and the 4 that is left makes one more group. So 104 divided by 4 is 26 swaps.
Every swap puts 3 apples in. So how do we find the number of apples?

ask.ifNot: There are 26 swaps, and each one adds 3 apples. That is 26 lots of 3.

beats.say: 26 times 3. 20 times 3 is 60, 6 times 3 is 18, and together that is 78 apples.
Does 78 make sense? Yes. Only 3 apples go in for every 4 mangoes that come out, so there should be fewer apples than there were mangoes.
Count the swaps first, by dividing. Then multiply by what each swap brings in.
A round bracket inside a curly bracket, and then a little minus 4 on the end.
What is the very first thing to work out?

ask.ifNot: We start inside the innermost bracket. And in there, times goes before plus. So 2 times 6 is the very first step.

beats.say: 2 times 6 is 12. Then 4 plus 12 is 16. The round bracket is done.
Now the curly bracket. 16 divided by 4 is 4.
And 4 minus 4 is 0.
Here is the trap they set. Adding 4 and 2 first gives 6 times 6, which is 36. Carry on from there and you reach 5, which is one of the choices!
Inside a bracket the same order still applies: times and divide before plus and minus. Then move outwards, bracket by bracket.
We want to write 12 minutes as a decimal part of an hour.
First as a fraction. 12 minutes is what fraction of an hour?

ask.ifNot: An hour has 60 minutes, not 100. So 12 minutes is 12 out of 60.

beats.say: 12 goes into 60 exactly 5 times. So 12 minutes is one fifth of an hour.
Now one fifth as a decimal. Decimals like tenths, so change it: one fifth is the same as 2 tenths, and 2 tenths is 0.2.
The choices show it as 0.20. That is the same number: a zero on the end of a decimal changes nothing.
Check: 0.2 of 60 minutes is 12 minutes. Yes.
The tempting slip is to write the 12 straight after the point. But minutes are sixtieths of an hour, so always divide by 60.
A college has girls and boys, in a commerce stream and a science stream. Lots of numbers, so let's take them one at a time.

board.text: Girls = 735, which is 145 less than the boys

beats.say: The girls are 145 less than the boys. So how do we find the number of boys?

ask.ifNot: The girls are the smaller group. So the boys are 145 more than the girls: start from 735 and add 145.

beats.say: 735 plus 145 is 880. There are 880 boys.
So the whole college is 880 boys plus 735 girls. That is 1615 students.
The commerce stream has 435 boys and 375 girls, which is 810 students.
Everyone who is not in commerce is in science. 1615 minus 810 is 805.
Let's check another way. Science boys: 880 minus 435 is 445. Science girls: 735 minus 375 is 360. And 445 plus 360 is 805.
In a long word problem, find one missing number at a time. And watch which group is the bigger one when you read less than.
Four sums made from 10 and 3. This time we want the greatest, so let's work out each one.
Start with the first, 10 minus 3 times 3. Which part goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times comes before minus. So 3 times 3 goes first, even though the minus is on the left.

beats.say: 3 times 3 is 9, and 10 minus 9 is 1.
The second has a bracket, and brackets go first. 10 plus 3 is 13, and 13 times 3 is 39.
The third: 10 times 3 is 30, and 30 plus 3 is 33.
The fourth: 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 plus 10 is 19.
So the values are 1, 39, 33 and 19. The greatest is 39, from the one with the bracket.
See what the bracket did? It made the 3 multiply the whole of 10 plus 3, not just one number. Work each choice in the proper order, then compare.
Krina meant to multiply by 2, but pressed times 20. We want one more step that puts it right.
Let's try it with a real number, so we can see what happened. Say her number was 7. She wanted 14, but the calculator shows 140.
140 instead of 14. How many times too big is her answer?

ask.ifNot: 20 is 10 times as big as 2. So her answer came out 10 times as big as it should be.

beats.say: To fix an answer that is 10 times too big, we divide by 10. But look at the choices: none of them says divide by 10!
Which of the choices does the same job as dividing by 10?

ask.ifNot: 0.1 is one tenth. Multiplying by one tenth means taking a tenth of the number, and that is exactly the same as dividing by 10.

beats.say: 140 times 0.1 is 14. So she should multiply by 0.1.
Why not divide by 20? That would undo the whole times 20 and leave just her starting number, 7. She still wants it doubled.
Remember: multiplying by 0.1 is the same as dividing by 10. And multiplying by 0.5 is the same as halving.
A square bracket with a round bracket inside it, and the little word of in the middle.
What is the very first thing to work out?

ask.ifNot: Innermost bracket first, and inside it times goes before minus. So 2 times 10 is the first step. Doing 25 minus 2 first is the classic slip.

beats.say: 2 times 10 is 20, and 25 minus 20 is 5. The round bracket is worth 5.
Now we meet 3 of 5. What does the word of tell us to do?

ask.ifNot: 3 of something means 3 lots of it. And lots of means multiply.

beats.say: 3 times 5 is 15. And of is done before the plus, just like times. So the square bracket is 5 plus 15, which is 20.
And 778 minus 20 is 758.
Brackets from the inside out. Inside each one, of and times and divide go first, then plus and minus.
A container holds 2 decagrams of medicine. We want to know how many doses of 1 milligram that is.
Two prefixes to unpack: deca and milli. Deca means 10, so one decagram is 10 grams. That makes 2 decagrams 20 grams.
Milli means a thousandth. So how many milligrams make one gram?

ask.ifNot: Milli means one thousandth. It takes 1000 thousandths to make one whole, so one gram is 1000 milligrams.

beats.say: One gram is 1000 milligrams.
So 20 grams is 20 times 1000 milligrams. That is 20000, so there are 20000 doses.
In one line, it is 2 times 10 times 1000. Notice we multiplied both times: going from a big unit to a small one, the number always grows.
Learn what the prefixes mean. Then change units one step at a time, through the plain gram in the middle.
X leaves 2 when divided by 5. Y leaves 4 when divided by 5. What does X plus Y leave?

board.text: X ÷ 5 leaves 2.  Y ÷ 5 leaves 4.  (X + Y) ÷ 5 leaves ?

beats.say: Picture X as some bundles of 5 with 2 loose ones. And Y as bundles of 5 with 4 loose ones. For example, 7 and 9.
When we add, bundles join bundles, and loose ones join loose ones. 2 loose plus 4 loose makes 6 loose.
6 loose ones. Can 6 be the remainder when we divide by 5?

choices: No: 6 is one more 5, and 1 over
ask.ifNot: A remainder must be smaller than the divisor. 6 loose ones can make one more bundle of 5, and that leaves just 1.

beats.say: 6 is one more 5, with 1 over. So the remainder is 1.
Check with our example. 7 plus 9 is 16, and 16 is 3 fives and 1 more.
So the remainder is 1, whatever X and Y are.
Add the remainders. If the total reaches the divisor, take out one more group. What is left is the new remainder.
We want to take away as little as possible from 13601, so that what is left divides exactly by 87.
Which number tells us what to take away?

ask.ifNot: A remainder is exactly the bit that spoils a division. Take the remainder away, and what is left divides perfectly.

beats.say: So let's divide 13601 by 87, in chunks. 87 times 100 is 8700. That leaves 4901.
87 times 50 is 4350. That leaves 551.
87 times 6 is 522. That leaves 29. And 29 is smaller than 87, so we stop here.
We used 100 and 50 and 6 lots of 87: that is 156 lots, with 29 left over.
So take away the 29. What is left, 13572, is exactly 87 times 156.
The least number to subtract is always the remainder. Divide, and the leftover is your answer.
Four decimals made of 7s and 0s, placed to confuse the eye. Let's add them safely.
Before adding decimals, what must we line up?

ask.ifNot: Each digit must sit under digits of the same place: tenths under tenths, ones under ones. Lining up the points does exactly that.

beats.say: So write each one with three decimal places, padding with zeros. Now every point sits in the same spot.
Add two at a time. 7.007 plus 0.07 is 7.077.
Add 70.7 to that. The 7 tenths drop into the empty tenths place, and we get 77.777. All sevens!
Last, add 70.07. Take care with the carries: 7 tens and 7 tens make more than 10 tens, so 1 goes into the hundreds place. We get 147.847.
A rough check. 7 plus 70 plus 70 is 147, and our answer is just a little more than that. Good.
With decimals, line up the points, pad with zeros, and add place by place.
Fractions of numbers, a bracket, and a 2 standing right outside it. Remember that of means multiply.
Brackets first. Inside is 2 fifths of 40. How do we find 2 fifths of 40?

ask.ifNot: Fifths means sharing into 5 equal parts. So divide 40 by 5 to get one fifth, then take 2 of those parts.

beats.say: 40 divided by 5 is 8, and 2 of those make 16. And one ninth of 27 is 27 divided by 9, which is 3.
So the bracket is 16 plus 3, which is 19.
Now the front. 5 sixths of 72: 72 divided by 6 is 12, and 5 of those make 60.
We are down to 60 minus 2 times 19. Which part goes first?

ask.ifNot: The 2 next to the bracket means times, and times comes before minus. So 2 times 19 goes first.

beats.say: 2 times 19 is 38. And 60 minus 38 is 22.
Read of as times. Do the bracket first, then times, and the minus right at the end.
This line is not true yet. One pair of brackets will make it equal 29.
Think backwards. If the plus 11 comes last, then everything before it must make 18. And there is a 36 in the line. What is 18 compared with 36?

ask.ifNot: 36 is 18 plus 18. So 18 is exactly half of 36.

beats.say: So we need half of 36. That means the part in front, 6 divided by something, should come to a half. 6 divided by 12 is a half.
Can we make 12 after the divide sign? Yes: 21 minus 9 is 12. So the brackets go round 21 minus 9.
Brackets first, giving 12. Then left to right: 6 divided by 12 is a half, and half of 36 is 18.
And 18 plus 11 is 29. The line is true now.
To place brackets, work backwards from the answer you need. Then look for numbers that can build the missing piece.
A two-digit number ending in 8, times a three-digit number ending in 6. The other digits are hidden. Which choice can be the product?
We cannot multiply hidden digits. But what can we say for certain about the product?

ask.ifNot: The last digit of the product depends only on the last digits of the two numbers, and those are showing: 8 and 6.

beats.say: 8 times 6 is 48, so the product must end in 8. That removes 79764, which ends in 4.
The other three all end in 8, so now test the size. The smallest numbers that fit are 18 and 106, and 18 times 106 is 1908.
1808 is below the smallest possible product, so it is out.
The biggest numbers that fit are 98 and 996, and 98 times 996 is 97608. That has five digits, so the six-digit 970608 is far too big.
Only 50808 is left. And it works: 58 times 876 is 50808.
Two tests for a hidden-digit product: the last digit, and then the smallest and biggest it could be.
We are given that 6.7 times 58 is 388.6. The new sum has the same digits, with the points in different places.
How did 6.7 turn into 0.67?

ask.ifNot: The point moved one place to the left. That makes a number 10 times smaller, which is dividing by 10.

beats.say: 6.7 was divided by 10. And 58 became 5.8, so it was divided by 10 as well.
Both numbers are 10 times smaller. So the product is 10 times 10 smaller, which is 100 times smaller.
Dividing by 100 moves the point two places to the left. 388.6 becomes 3.886.
Does that feel right? About two thirds of nearly 6 should be close to 4. And 3.886 is.
Keep the digits from the fact you were given. Then work out how much smaller each number became, and shrink the answer by both.
Four big numbers to add. Before you start, look at the digits. Something is going on.
Read down each column of the table. What do you notice?

ask.ifNot: Read down any column. You will find a 1, a 2, a 3 and a 4, just in a different order each time.

beats.say: So every column adds up to the same thing: 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4, which is 10.
Units column: 10. Write 0, carry 1. Tens column: 10, plus the carried 1, is 11. Write 1, carry 1.
The hundreds do just the same: 11, write 1, carry 1. And the thousands make 11 as well, which we write in full.
Reading the digits off: 11110.
Another way to see it. Every place holds 10, so the total is 10 lots of 1111.
Before a big addition, look down the columns. A pattern can turn four long numbers into one small sum.
A product on top, divided by a sum underneath. Let's write the top and the bottom separately.
Bottom first, it is easier. Pair the ends: 1 plus 8 is 9, and 2 plus 7 is 9 as well. Every pair makes 9. How many pairs do 8 numbers make?

ask.ifNot: Each pair uses up 2 numbers. So 8 numbers make 4 pairs.

beats.say: 4 pairs of 9 make 36. So the bottom is 36.
Now the top. Don't multiply it out yet! We are going to divide by 36, and 36 is 6 times 6. The top has a 6. Which two other numbers on top make another 6?

ask.ifNot: 2 times 3 is 6. So the 2, the 3 and the 6 on top multiply to 36 between them.

beats.say: So 2 times 3 times 6 is 36, and that cancels with the 36 underneath.
What is left on top? 1, 4, 5 and 7. 4 times 5 is 20, and 20 times 7 is 140.
The long way agrees. The top multiplies out to 5040, and 5040 divided by 36 is 140.
When a big product is divided by something, look for that something hiding among the factors. Cancel first, multiply after.
A bracket with fractions of numbers inside it, and then a divide by a fraction. One piece at a time.
Brackets first, and inside the bracket, of means multiply. How do we find 3 fifths of 25?

ask.ifNot: Fifths means sharing into 5 equal parts. So divide 25 by 5 to find one fifth, then take 3 of those parts.

beats.say: 25 divided by 5 is 5, and 3 of those make 15. In the same way, 39 divided by 13 is 3, and 7 of those make 21.
So the bracket is 9 plus 15, minus 21. That leaves 3.
Now we must divide 3 by 4 thirds. What is the trick for dividing by a fraction?

ask.ifNot: To divide by a fraction, turn it upside down and multiply. So dividing by 4 thirds becomes multiplying by 3 quarters.

beats.say: 3 times 3 quarters is 9 quarters.
8 quarters make 2 wholes, and there is one quarter more. That is 2 and a quarter, or 2.25.
Bracket first, reading of as times. And to divide by a fraction, flip it and multiply.
We want to know what part of a whole day 216 minutes is, written as a decimal.
First we need a whole day in minutes. Which sum gives that?

ask.ifNot: A day has 24 hours, and each hour has 60 minutes. So it is 24 lots of 60.

beats.say: 24 times 60 is 1440 minutes in a day. So our fraction is 216 out of 1440.
Big numbers, so shrink it in steps. Divide the top and bottom by 12, and we get 18 out of 120. Divide by 6, and we get 3 out of 20.
Now turn 3 twentieths into a decimal. What should we change the 20 into?

ask.ifNot: Decimals count in tenths and hundredths. 20 goes into 100 exactly 5 times, so twentieths can be turned into hundredths.

beats.say: Multiply the top and the bottom by 5. 3 twentieths becomes 15 hundredths, which is 0.15.
Check: 0.15 of 1440 minutes should be 216 minutes. It is.
Put both amounts in the same unit, write the fraction, simplify it, and then change it to hundredths.
We add 3042 and 869, then take a mystery number away, and we are left with 2165. What was taken away?
First the sum. Add the 869 in two bites. 3042 plus 800 is 3842, and 69 more makes 3911.
So we start at 3911, take something away, and land on 2165. How do we find the something?

ask.ifNot: Look at the bar. The whole is 3911 and one part is 2165. The other part is what is left when we take 2165 away from 3911.

beats.say: 3911 minus 2000 is 1911. Then take away the other 165, and we get 1746.
So the number to subtract is 1746.
Check by adding back. 1746 plus 2165 is 3911, our sum. It fits.
When a whole is split into two parts and you know one, subtract to get the other. A quick bar makes that easy to see.
We are given a multiplication fact, but asked a division with decimals. The digits match, so the fact will do the heavy work.
First turn the fact into a division. Which division does it give us?

ask.ifNot: If 168 lots of 54 make 9072, then 9072 shared into 168 equal parts gives 54 in each.

beats.say: So 9072 divided by 168 is 54. Now for the decimal points.
9072 became 0.9072: the point moved four places, so it was divided by 10000. And 168 became 16.8, divided by 10.
The number being shared is 10000 times smaller, so the answer shrinks 10000 times. But the divisor is 10 times smaller too. What does a smaller divisor do to the answer?

ask.ifNot: Sharing among fewer gives each one more. So when the divisor gets 10 times smaller, the answer gets 10 times bigger.

beats.say: 10000 times smaller, then 10 times bigger. Overall, the answer is 1000 times smaller than 54. That is 0.054.
Check by multiplying back. 16.8 times 0.054 gives 0.9072. Just right.
In a division, shrinking the first number shrinks the answer, but shrinking the divisor makes the answer grow. Track both.
This line is not true yet. One pair of brackets will make it equal 19.
As it stands, we go left to right: 42 divided by 7 is 6, times 2, plus 16, comes to 28. Too big.
Think backwards from 19. If the plus 16 comes last, then just before it we had 3. So 42 divided by something must be 3. Divided by what?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 14 is 42. So 42 divided by 14 gives 3.

beats.say: We need to divide by 14. And 7 times 2 is 14! So the brackets go round 7 times 2.
Brackets first: 7 times 2 is 14. Then 42 divided by 14 is 3.
And 3 plus 16 is 19. The line is true now.
Here is something worth noticing. Divide and times are equally strong, so without brackets the divide on the left goes first. The brackets let the times jump the queue.
To place brackets, work backwards from the answer, and find which numbers can build the piece you need.
A long line with no brackets at all. It looks scary, but it breaks into pieces.
The minus and the plus split the line into three chunks. What do we do first: the chunks, or the minus and plus between them?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide come before plus and minus. So each chunk is worked out on its own first.

beats.say: First chunk, left to right. 21 goes into 84 exactly 4 times, so 21 divided by 84 is one quarter. And a quarter of 16 is 4.
Second chunk: 7 times 3 is 21.
Third chunk: 306 divided by 17. 17 times 10 is 170 and 17 times 8 is 136. Together they make 306, so the answer is 18.
The line is now 4 minus 21 plus 18. But 4 minus 21 dips below zero. Is there a friendlier way?

ask.ifNot: The minus belongs only to the 21. So we may bring the plus 18 forward: 4 plus 18, and then take away 21.

beats.say: 4 plus 18 is 22, and 22 minus 21 is 1.
Split a long line at its plus and minus signs. Work out each chunk, then put the chunks together.
Four decimals built from 8s and 0s. They look alike, so the danger is letting a digit slip into a place where it does not belong.
We will give every number three decimal places, so the points line up. What does 0.08 become?

ask.ifNot: Padding means writing zeros at the end, after the last digit. So 0.08 becomes 0.080. A zero slipped in front of the 8 would change its value.

beats.say: Here they are, padded and lined up on the point.
Add two at a time. 8.008 plus 0.08 is 8.088.
Add 80.8 to that. The 8 tenths drop into the empty tenths place, and we get 88.888. All eights!
Last, add 80.08. Take care: 8 tens and 8 tens make more than 10 tens, so 1 goes into the hundreds place. We get 168.968.
A rough check. 8 plus 80 plus 80 is 168, and our answer is just a little more than that. Good.
With decimals, line up the points, pad with zeros at the end, and add place by place.
2000 is divided by a mystery number, giving 29 with 57 left over. We need that divisor, and then its square.
Write the division the other way round: divisor times quotient, plus remainder. What do the equal groups add up to, without the leftover?

ask.ifNot: The 57 is what was left after the groups were made. Take it away from 2000 and we have exactly the groups.

beats.say: 2000 minus 57 is 1943. So the mystery number times 29 is 1943.
How many 29s are in 1943? 29 times 60 is 1740. That leaves 203, and 203 is 29 times 7.
60 and 7 make 67. So the divisor is 67. And that fits: the remainder, 57, is smaller than 67.
Are we finished?

ask.ifNot: 67 is the divisor. But the question asks for the square of the divisor, so one more step.

beats.say: 67 times 67. 67 times 60 is 4020, and 67 times 7 is 469. Together, 4489.
Take the remainder off, divide by the quotient to get the divisor, and then do whatever the question asks with it.
One division fact is given, and a second division is asked. The digits are the same, so we will reuse the fact.
The new sum divides by 6.8, which looks like the 68, not like the 12.75. So first swap the fact around. 867 divided by 68 is what?

ask.ifNot: In a division fact, the divisor and the answer can swap places. 867 divided by 12.75 gives 68, so 867 divided by 68 gives 12.75.

beats.say: 867 divided by 68 is 12.75. Now look at the decimal points.
867 became 8.67, so it was divided by 100. And 68 became 6.8, divided by 10.
The first number is 100 times smaller, which makes the answer 100 times smaller. But the divisor is 10 times smaller, which makes the answer 10 times bigger. Overall: 10 times smaller.
So take 12.75 and make it 10 times smaller. The point moves one place to the left: 1.275.
Does it feel right? 8.67 is a little more than 6.8, so the answer should be a little more than 1. And it is.
Reuse the given fact. Then track each decimal point: a smaller first number shrinks the answer, a smaller divisor grows it.
Three boxes to fill with signs, so that the line comes to 16. We will test each set of signs.
First set: times, minus, divide. That would need 3 divided by 14, which is not a whole number. So it cannot land exactly on 16.
Second set: minus, divide, plus. Which part of this goes first?

ask.ifNot: Divide comes before plus and minus. So 6 divided by 3 goes first, though it sits in the middle.

beats.say: 6 divided by 3 is 2. Then 12 minus 2, plus 14, is 24. Not 16.
Third set: times, divide, plus. 12 times 6 is 72, divided by 3 is 24, and adding 14 gives 38. Not 16 either.
Fourth set: plus, times, minus. Times first: 6 times 3 is 18. Then 12 plus 18 is 30, and 30 minus 14 is 16. That is the one!
So the signs are plus, times, minus. Test every set, and each time do times and divide before plus and minus.
We multiply all the one-digit odd numbers together, divide by 18, and want to know what is left over.
Which are the one-digit odd numbers?

ask.ifNot: One-digit numbers go up to 9. The odd ones among them are 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. Don't leave out the 1 or the 9.

beats.say: Multiply them a step at a time. 1 times 3 times 5 is 15. Then 15 times 7 is 105. Then 105 times 9 is 945.
Now divide 945 by 18, in chunks. 18 times 50 is 900. That leaves 45.
18 times 2 is 36. That leaves 9. And 9 is smaller than 18, so we stop.
So 945 is 52 lots of 18, with 9 left over. The remainder is 9.
A neat sense check. 945 is odd, and any number of 18s is even. So the leftover has to be odd. That fits our 9.
For a remainder, take out the divisor in big easy chunks until what is left is smaller than the divisor.
Four decimals, with minus and plus signs mixed together.
Going left to right, we would start by taking 14.659 from 2.007, and dip below zero. There is a friendlier way. Which two numbers are being taken away?

ask.ifNot: Each number owns the sign in front of it. The minus signs sit in front of 14.659 and 2.042.

beats.say: So gather them into two teams. The ones we add, and the ones we take away.
The adding team: 2.007 plus 16.317 is 18.324.
The taking-away team: 14.659 plus 2.042 is 16.701.
Now one subtraction. 18.324 minus 16 is 2.324, and taking away the other 0.701 leaves 1.623.
A rough check with whole numbers: 2 minus 15, plus 16, minus 2 is 1. Our answer is a bit more than 1. Good.
When plus and minus are mixed, add up everything with a plus, add up everything with a minus, and subtract once.
A bracket in the middle and a little chain of times and divide on the end.
Where do we start?

ask.ifNot: Brackets come before everything else. So we work out the inside of the bracket first.

beats.say: Inside the bracket, times and divide go before the plus. 20 times 7 is 140. 150 divided by 3 is 50.
140 plus 50 is 190. So the whole bracket is worth 190.
The bracket is gone. What comes next?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide still come before plus and minus. So the 8 times 2 divided by 8 at the end is next.

beats.say: 8 times 2 is 16, and 16 divided by 8 is 2. Times 8 and divide by 8 undo each other, so only the 2 is left.
Now left to right. 200 minus 190 is 10, and 10 plus 2 is 12.
Bracket first. Then times and divide. Then plus and minus, from left to right.
Two jobs here. Multiply 7.2 by 3.9, then see how much more that is than the smallest 2-digit prime number.
First the product. Forget the points for a moment and do 72 times 39. 72 times 40 is 2880, and one 72 less is 2808.
Now put the point back. 7.2 and 3.9 have one decimal place each. How many decimal places does the product have?

ask.ifNot: One decimal place in each number makes two altogether. So the product has two decimal places.

beats.say: So 2808 becomes 28.08. That feels right, because 7 times 4 is 28.
Next, what is the smallest 2-digit prime number?

ask.ifNot: 10 is the smallest 2-digit number, but it divides by 2 and by 5, so it is not prime. The next one, 11, divides only by 1 and itself.

beats.say: It is 11. And 28.08 minus 11 is 17.08.
To multiply decimals, multiply as whole numbers, then count the decimal places to put the point back.
Two three-digit numbers, one ending in 7 and one ending in 6. Stars hide the rest. Which choice can be their product?
Start with what we can see: the last digits, 7 and 6. What must the product end in?

ask.ifNot: Multiply the two last digits, 7 and 6, and look at the digit that answer ends in. That is the last digit of the product.

beats.say: 7 times 6 is 42, so the product ends in 2. That removes 457647, which ends in 7.
Three are left, all ending in 2. So test the size. The smallest numbers that fit are 107 and 106, and 107 times 106 is 11342.
11332 is just below that. So close, but too small. Out.

beats.say: We need to divide by 32. Can we build 32 from the 12, the 3 and the 4? 12 times 3 is 36, and 36 minus 4 is 32. Yes!
So the brackets go round 12 times 3 minus 4. Brackets first gives 32, and 192 divided by 32 is 6.

The shorter bracket, round 12 times 3 only, would mean dividing 192 by 36, and that does not come out whole. The longer one is needed.
To place brackets, work backwards from the answer, and build the number you need from the ones that are there.
